source.title: DBAT: Dynamic Backward Attention Transformer for Material Segmentation with Cross-Resolution Patches
source.authors: Yuwen Heng; S. Dasmahapatra; Hansung Kim

record.tranche_reason: The study uses network dissection to measure semantic-concept alignments of neurons in vision models. This bears conceptually on V4, but it does not measure the total share of interpretable neurons or test whether better tools increase that share.
record.gate_note: The network-dissection results are the only results relevant to the listed versions. Segmentation accuracy, ablations, attention analysis and CKA results do not test them. The network-dissection figures show concept-specific percentages, not a total interpretable-neuron share; the paper gives qualitative observations but no numerical values for those plots in the text.
record.test_reason: This is a material-segmentation paper. It uses network dissection only to see which Broden concept types (texture, object, part, and so on) its own and comparison models' last-layer neurons align with. It never measures the overall share of interpretable neurons. It does not compare tools or architectures to see whether that share changes, and it does not touch language models, explanation validity or circuits. Its one remark on the claim, that only a fraction of neurons can be aligned and some detect mixed features, is stated without measurement. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The main conclusion is that DBAT reaches the best accuracy among real-time models (86.85% Pixel Acc on LMD) with narrow uncertainty across runs. The interpretability analyses (attention masks, CKA, network dissection) are used to argue that DBAT draws on cross-resolution patches and is especially good at texture features. The authors also note that dissection explains only disentangled neurons.
record.recipe_differences: Uses network dissection on vision models and Broden semantic labels, rather than testing textual neuron explanations on held-out activations or scoring their predictions on new text.
record.method_sensitivity: Pre-training and task/dataset are compared; the authors report that pre-training changes concept alignments and that object-task models differ from material-task models.

fits_no_version.finding: The kinds of concepts that last-encoder-layer neurons align with (texture, object, part) shift with pre-training, training task (material vs object) and architecture. EfficientNet-b5, for example, has almost no texture neurons. Values are figure-only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The concept types that dissected vision neurons align with depend on training task, pre-training and architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors state, without measuring it, that network dissection aligns only a fraction of channels. They say the rest detect useful but mixed features, such as texture-object combinations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under network dissection, many vision neurons remain unaligned to single concepts (unquantified assertion).

record.problems: The evidence is from vision networks, not language models. Network dissection aligns neurons to a fixed set of semantic concepts rather than testing whether a human-readable explanation predicts neuron activations on held-out inputs. The paper states that only a fraction of neurons can be aligned and that mixed-feature neurons may remain unexplained; the concept-alignment plots provide no text-stated overall share or uncertainty.

untested.parts: All: Qwen3-32B pole audit and its one-job, two-job and unexplained shares.
All: other language models, dense and mixture-of-experts, scale.
All: InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition.
Overall interpretable-neuron share and whether it rises with better tools, modern architectures or regularization. The paper only reports which concept types aligned neurons prefer.
All: neuron attribution graphs and reconstruction error.
All: whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on new inputs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V4 links is wrong. The dissection results describe concept-type preferences for the authors' own model and comparison models, not the share of interpretable neurons or the effect of tools on it. No row should link to any version. There are no numeric values in the text for Figures 10–11. The Fig 10(b) Swin-on-ADE20K comparison has no row, but it is not relevant to any version.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole-level audit, one-job/two-job shares, and explanations tested on held-out activations.
Language-model scaling, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and models up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, shared pose feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.

The study compares concept alignments across vision models and training tasks, but does not test the effects of tools or regularization, estimate an overall interpretable-neuron share, or study InceptionV1-sized models.
Attribution graphs, model-behavior explanation, and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples predict firing on new inputs.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: DBAT
rows.operation_detail: Network dissection aligns last-encoder-layer neurons with semantic concepts.
rows.measure: Percentage of neurons aligned to semantic concepts
rows.note: Text says this DBAT shows a preference for texture features and that portions of its neurons align with object and scene features. The plot does not provide a text-stated total share of interpretable neurons.
rows.check: Measures how aligned neurons spread across concept types, not the share of interpretable neurons or any tool or architecture effect on it. Values are figure-only.

rows.measure: Percentage of neurons aligned to semantic concepts
rows.note: Text says the pre-trained DBAT has more neurons aligned to texture and object features than the DBAT without pre-training; no overall interpretable-neuron share is stated.
rows.check: Effect of pre-training on the concept-type spread, not on an interpretable-neuron share. Figure-only.
